title: Head Coverings and the Lord's Supper
summary: After urging the Corinthians to imitate him as he imitates Christ, Paul addresses two problems in their worship. First, he instructs men and women who pray and prophesy about covering or uncovering the head, grounding his argument in headship, creation, custom, and nature. Second, he rebukes the way they celebrate the Lord's Supper, where the rich eat and drink while the poor go hungry, and he recalls Jesus's words at the Last Supper and warns them to examine themselves and wait for one another.
story: Verse 1 closes the argument of chapters 8 to 10, where Paul had held up his own example of seeking others' good. From verse 2 onward the letter turns to the church's gatherings for worship, a subject that continues through chapter 14. This chapter handles conduct at the gathering (who covers the head, how the meal is shared); chapters 12 to 14 will handle spiritual gifts in worship. Both halves of this chapter concern honor and shame in the assembly, and both show the Corinthians treating worship as a stage for status rather than a place of mutual care. The Supper passage also contains the earliest written account of Jesus's words at the Last Supper.
historical:
Christians in Corinth met in private homes, since church buildings did not exist for another two centuries. A well-to-do house had a formal dining room (the triclinium), where guests reclined on couches, holding perhaps nine to a dozen people, and a larger courtyard or hall (the atrium) where others could gather. Roman dinner customs openly ranked guests: the host's friends of higher status reclined in the dining room and received better food and wine, while others were served elsewhere and less. Many scholars think that pattern explains verses 20 to 22: the wealthy, who could arrive early, began their meal and ate well, while slaves and laborers who came later found little left.

Paul's account of the Last Supper (verses 23 to 26) was written around AD 53 to 55, probably before any of the Gospels, and he describes it as a tradition he “received” and “passed on,” technical terms for handing down teaching. It closely matches Luke 22:19-20, and both include the command to do this in remembrance of Jesus.
cultural:
Head coverings carried social meaning in the Roman world, though scholars debate the details. Roman men drew the fold of their toga over their heads when offering sacrifice, as statues of Augustus as priest show, so a covered male head in prayer might have looked like pagan priestly practice. Respectable married women were generally expected to cover their heads in public, as a sign of modesty and of being married; an uncovered head or loosened hair could suggest immodesty, and some ecstatic cults had women worship with hair unbound. In a church meeting in a home, where public and private space blurred, the question of what women and men should do with their heads while praying or prophesying aloud was a real one.

Honor and shame governed the ancient world. Paul's language is saturated with it: to dishonor the head, to be a disgrace, to be one's glory. The Supper problem is likewise one of shame: by eating their fine food while others went hungry, the wealthy “humiliate those who have nothing” (verse 22). A meal meant to proclaim the Lord's death had become a display of social rank.
literary: The two sections are bracketed by praise and its absence: “I commend you” (verse 2) and “I have no praise to offer” (verse 17). The head-covering argument is compressed and layered: a principle about heads (verse 3), a case for men and women (verses 4 to 6), an argument from creation (verses 7 to 10), a qualification “in the Lord” that stresses mutual dependence (verses 11 and 12), and appeals to propriety, nature, and the practice of the churches (verses 13 to 16). The Supper section follows a clear four-step movement: the problem (verses 17 to 22), the tradition (verses 23 to 26), the consequences (verses 27 to 32), and a practical solution (verses 33 and 34).

outline.t: Imitate me as I imitate Christ
Heads and head coverings in prayer and prophecy
Creation, glory, and mutual dependence in the Lord
Propriety, nature, and the practice of the churches
The tradition of the Last Supper
Eating in an unworthy manner and self-examination

doctrines.note: Christians read this passage in different ways. Roman Catholic teaching holds that the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood (transubstantiation); Lutherans confess Christ's true body and blood present in, with, and under the elements; Reformed churches teach a real spiritual feeding on Christ by faith; and many Baptist and free churches stress a memorial meal of remembrance and proclamation. All agree the meal proclaims “the Lord's death until He comes” (verse 26) and must be received with self-examination and love.

Paul speaks of an order in creation (verses 3 and 7 to 9) and in the same breath insists that “in the Lord” woman and man are not independent of each other, and that “everything comes from God” (verses 11 and 12). Women pray and prophesy aloud (verse 5), and most interpreters take the setting to be the gathered church.
Despising the poor at the Lord's table is despising “the church of God” (verse 22). The Supper is a meal of one family, and it is profaned when it reproduces the world's hierarchies.

God's judgment on the church's abuse of the Supper is disciplinary, meant to keep believers “so that we will not be condemned with the world” (verse 32). Self-examination now spares believers judgment later.

words.note: Kephale, head, used nine times in the chapter, both literally (the physical head) and figuratively (verse 3). Scholars debate the figurative sense: many take it to mean authority over, others argue for source or origin (as with the head of a river), and others for the prominent or preeminent one. The choice shapes how verse 3 relates to the rest of the passage and to the wider debate about roles of men and women.

Paradosis, tradition, a teaching handed on. Paul praises the Corinthians for keeping the traditions (verse 2) and then hands on the most important one, the words of the Supper, using the paired verbs of receiving and passing on (verse 23), the same pair he uses for the gospel in 15:3.

Anamnesis, remembrance. In Jewish worship, remembering meant more than recalling; at Passover each generation remembered the exodus as its own rescue. “Do this in remembrance of Me” calls the church to make Christ's saving death present to its faith and life, though traditions explain that presence differently.

Diakrino, to discern, distinguish, or judge. Verse 29 warns against eating “without recognizing the body” (a form of this verb), and verse 31 uses it for judging ourselves. Some take “the body” as Christ's body given in the bread; others as the church, the body the wealthy were despising; many think Paul holds both together.

christ: The chapter holds the earliest written record of Jesus's words at his last meal: “This is My body, which is for you” and “This cup is the new covenant in My blood” (verses 24 and 25). The new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31 is sealed by Christ's death, and every celebration of the Supper is a way to “proclaim the Lord's death until He comes” (verse 26), looking back to the cross and forward to his return. The chapter's first verse makes Christ the pattern of Christian conduct, and verse 3 places even Christ in relation to God as his head, a verse theologians have read in light of the Son's willing obedience to the Father, not as making him less than God.

hard.q: Should women cover their heads in worship today, and what is Paul's argument really about?
hard.a:
This is one of the most debated passages in Paul, and Christians differ at several points. On practice, the historic majority of the church, from the early centuries into the twentieth, expected women to cover their heads in worship, and some churches (including many Anabaptist, Brethren, and some Orthodox and traditional Catholic communities) still do, arguing that Paul grounds the practice in creation and angels, not merely in custom. Most churches today read the covering as a cultural expression of a lasting principle: that men and women should honor God and each other in worship, and not blur the distinction between them. A third view takes Paul's point in verse 15 (“long hair is given to her as a covering”) to mean the covering is a woman's hair itself, so the passage concerns hair length or style.

On meaning, readers disagree about kephale (see the word note), and so about whether the passage teaches an order of authority in the home and church, a complementarian reading, or an order of origin that is balanced by mutuality in the Lord, an egalitarian reading. “Because of the angels” (verse 10) is also unclear: most think of angels present at worship as guardians of order, while others connect it to the fallen angels of Genesis 6. What is clear is that women were praying and prophesying aloud (most take the setting to be the gathered church, though a few place it in smaller household meetings), that Paul cared about honor and gender distinction, and that he balanced order with mutual dependence. These are second-order questions on which faithful churches differ.

questions: Paul says the Corinthians' meal was not really the Lord's Supper because the poor were humiliated. What would it take for the Lord's table in your church to reflect the gospel's equality?
What does it mean for you to examine yourself before coming to the Lord's Supper, and how is that different from feeling unworthy to come?
The head-covering debate asks how to tell timeless principles from cultural forms. How do you make that judgment when reading Scripture?
